paragraphs: Mediation analysis asks how a treatment changes an outcome through intermediate variables. Most existing work considers a single treatment at one time. This paper addresses settings where treatments arrive repeatedly and their consequences unfold over time, such as mobile health. It introduces a reinforcement learning framework for evaluating mediation effects over an infinite horizon.

The framework separates the average treatment effect along two dimensions: whether an effect is immediate or delayed, and whether it passes through a mediator or acts directly. This produces four components. The distinction matters because a treatment can affect the current outcome and also influence later outcomes through different causal pathways.

After identifying these components, the authors develop estimators described as robust and semiparametrically efficient. These support statistical inference about the separate effects within the proposed framework. The paper reports supporting theoretical results, extensive numerical studies, and an application to mobile health data. Its contribution is a way to study both the timing and the pathways of treatment effects when interventions continue over time.
icml-2023-a-reinforcement-learning-frame.tldr: A reinforcement learning framework separates ongoing treatment effects into immediate and delayed contributions, both direct and mediated.

paragraphs: A Tucker decomposition represents a multidimensional array using a smaller core and associated factors. Under a size budget, choosing the core's dimensions is itself an optimization problem: different shapes allocate representational capacity differently and can produce different reconstruction errors. This paper studies how to choose that shape, also called the multilinear rank.

The authors connect reconstruction quality to higher-order singular values and introduce a related Tucker packing problem. They prove that this packing problem is NP-hard, then provide a polynomial-time approximation scheme through a connection to a two-dimensional knapsack problem with a matroid constraint. Their approach gives provable approximation guarantees for reconstruction error and extends to tree tensor network decompositions.

For practical evaluation, they implement their algorithm with an integer programming solver. Its solution quality is competitive with, and sometimes better than, a greedy method that evaluates the actual Tucker decomposition loss at each step. Reported speedups reach 1000 times. This suggests that selecting core shapes through the proposed optimization formulation can substantially reduce computation while retaining strong reconstruction quality in the evaluated cases.
icml-2023-approximately-optimal-core-sha.tldr: An approximation approach selects tensor decomposition core shapes with reconstruction guarantees and reported speedups of up to 1000 times.

paragraphs: Simulation-based inference uses simulated data to infer the unknown parameters behind observations. A challenge arises when inference must combine several observations. Methods that directly learn posterior distributions can require many simulator calls, while methods that learn likelihoods can combine observations more naturally but depend on additional inference procedures with their own performance drawbacks.

This paper proposes conditional score modeling as a way to combine useful properties of both approaches. It learns scores associated with diffused posterior distributions for individual observations. These scores describe local directions in the modeled distributions. The method then combines the learned scores to approximately generate samples from the posterior conditioned on multiple observations.

The important separation is between learning from individual observations and aggregating evidence at inference time. The authors describe their approach as sample-efficient and able to incorporate multiple observations naturally, without relying on the standard MCMC or variational inference procedures discussed in the comparison. The resulting samples are approximate: the contribution is a compositional route to posterior sampling, rather than a claim of exact inference.
icml-2023-compositional-score-modeling-f.tldr: Combining learned scores for individual observations enables sample-efficient, approximate posterior sampling from multiple observations.

paragraphs: A feature can be useful in one situation and misleading in another. The paper illustrates this with surrounding traffic: copying another car's speed could encourage running a red light, yet that same speed could reveal an otherwise unseen pedestrian. Treating the feature as permanently trustworthy or permanently irrelevant loses this distinction.

The authors formalize this problem as contextual reliability, where the appropriate features depend on the context. They propose Explicit Non-spurious feature Prediction, or ENP, as a two-stage approach. It first identifies which features are relevant in a particular context, then trains a prediction model to depend exclusively on those selected features.

This changes the target of robustness from ignoring a fixed set of suspicious signals to deciding when each signal is appropriate. The paper analyzes ENP theoretically, reports empirical advantages over existing methods, and introduces benchmarks for the setting. The findings support context-dependent feature selection as a useful response to spurious correlations when a single global division between reliable and unreliable features is inadequate.
icml-2023-contextual-reliability-when-di.tldr: ENP improves contextual reliability by identifying which features matter in each context and restricting predictions to those features.

paragraphs: This paper asks how much language modeling performance is achievable with a tightly limited training budget: one day on a single consumer GPU. The authors train a transformer from scratch using masked language modeling and evaluate its downstream performance. The motivation is to make meaningful pretraining experiments accessible when large computing resources are unavailable.

They revisit nearly every component of the pretraining pipeline and provide a modified pipeline whose performance is close to BERT. The investigation also asks why reducing the computing budget is difficult and which training or architectural changes actually help under this constraint. A technique's usefulness is therefore assessed within the specified time and hardware budget.

The authors find evidence that performance in this small-compute setting closely follows scaling laws observed with much larger budgets. They use those relationships to organize and assess recent improvements, including their practical suitability for constrained training. The result is both a concrete training pipeline and an analysis of how to spend limited computation effectively, with code provided for reproducing the experiments.
icml-2023-cramming-training-a-language-m.tldr: A redesigned pretraining pipeline achieves performance close to BERT after one day of training from scratch on one consumer GPU.

paragraphs: This paper starts with a trained black-box model and progressively extracts interpretable models from it. The motivation is to combine the flexibility of a black box with predictions that can be explained directly. Rather than asking one interpretable model to cover every input, the method lets different models specialize in different subsets of data.

Each iteration creates interpretable models and a residual network. The interpretable components select samples and explain them through first-order logic using concepts from the original model. Samples left over go to the flexible residual network. The process repeats on that residual until the interpretable components cover the desired proportion of data.

The experiments report diverse, instance-specific concepts with high concept completeness without compromising predictive performance. Residual networks also expose samples that are relatively harder to explain. The approach outperforms interpretable-by-design models during test-time interventions and can repair a shortcut learned by the original black box. These findings connect explanation with restructuring model behavior, while allowing the requested level of interpretable coverage to guide the process.
icml-2023-dividing-and-conquering-a-blac.tldr: Repeatedly extracting specialized interpretable models from a black box provides explanations while leaving harder cases to residual networks.

paragraphs: Federated analytics can aggregate information across users while communicating compact summaries. This paper studies two tasks under a linear sketching constraint: discovering frequently occurring items and approximately estimating an open-domain histogram. Motivated by secure aggregation across multiple rounds, it asks how much communication each task requires for a given level of accuracy.

The authors propose algorithms using local subsampling and invertible Bloom look-up tables. They show that these algorithms are information-theoretically optimal within a broad class of interactive schemes. Their analysis also identifies a cost of the linear sketching requirement: for both tasks, communication gains an additional linear dependence on the number of users participating in a round.

The two tasks differ substantially in how their communication costs depend on the number of rounds. For heavy-hitter discovery, that dependence is at most logarithmic; for approximate histograms, it scales with the square root of the number of rounds. Empirical results support the theoretical findings. The separation matters because finding common items and estimating their distribution impose different communication demands in the studied setting.
icml-2023-federated-heavy-hitter-recover.tldr: Optimal linear-sketching algorithms reveal different multi-round communication costs for discovering frequent items and estimating histograms.

paragraphs: Adversarial training seeks models that remain accurate under adversarial perturbations, but improving robustness with additional data can be expensive. Guided Adversarial Training, or GAT, instead adds learning tasks to a limited training dataset. The idea is to obtain more useful supervision from available examples while reducing reliance on collecting additional examples.

GAT turns a single-task model into a multitask model during adversarial training's min-max optimization. It guides optimization through a regularizer involving gradient curvature across tasks. Auxiliary tasks come from two sources: self-supervised tasks with automatically generated labels, and tasks based on domain knowledge with labels supplied by human experts.

Under limited data, the reported CIFAR-10 robust accuracy rises from 11% to 42%, while CheXpert robust AUC rises from 50% to 83%. On full CIFAR-10, GAT outperforms eight state-of-the-art adversarial training strategies. Across five datasets and six tasks, the results support task augmentation as an efficient alternative to data augmentation and as a possible way to improve both ordinary and adversarial performance.
icml-2023-gat-guided-adversarial-trainin.tldr: GAT uses auxiliary tasks to improve adversarial robustness, with substantial reported gains when training data is limited.

paragraphs: Fairness assessment becomes more complicated when a protected attribute varies continuously. This paper examines how to measure dependence involving such attributes and how to express the forms of dependence an application should permit. Its starting point is the Hirschfeld-Gebelein-Renyi indicator, or HGR, which the authors find valuable but limited in meaning, interpretability, and robustness.

The authors introduce a family of alternative indicators with semantics that complement HGR. They describe these indicators as transparent, interpretable, robust with finite samples, and configurable for particular applications. The contribution therefore concerns both the numerical measurement of dependence and the ability to understand what a chosen measurement represents.

The framework also supports fine-grained constraints that allow some types of dependence while disallowing others. This matters when an application's fairness requirements cannot be captured by a single undifferentiated restriction on dependence. The paper expands the available ways to specify fairness over continuous protected attributes, giving practitioners more control over which relationships their constraints target rather than presenting one universal fairness definition.
icml-2023-generalized-disparate-impact-f.tldr: A configurable family of fairness indicators supports interpretable constraints that selectively permit or forbid dependence on continuous protected attributes.

paragraphs: Harmonic functions appear in limiting cases of several major physical equations, including equations governing electromagnetism, fluids, heat, and waves. They also have applications in industrial optimization, robotic path planning, and random-walk exit times. This paper asks how neural networks can represent this important class of functions more effectively.

The central direction is to incorporate a preference for harmonic functions into the model, using the mathematical structure of the target functions to guide representation. The authors demonstrate effective ways to represent harmonic functions with neural networks. They also extend their results to quantum neural networks, showing that the approach applies across both of these model settings.

The paper compares the proposed approaches with physics-informed neural networks, including quantum versions, and reports favorable performance. Those findings support the usefulness of representations designed around harmonic structure in the evaluated problems. The broader motivation is that known properties of a function class can guide neural modeling, especially when that same class appears across several scientific and computational applications.
icml-2023-harmonic-neural-networks-29b82.tldr: Neural representations tailored to harmonic functions show favorable benchmark performance in both classical and quantum settings.

paragraphs: This paper constructs transformers that act as programmable computers by setting specific weights and repeatedly running the network in a loop. The input sequence serves as a program and memory, containing instructions together with locations for reading and writing data. Computation is organized through repeated execution of a fixed network.

The authors show that a constant number of encoder layers can emulate computing components such as nonlinear functions, function calls, program counters, conditional branches, and lexicographic operations. They combine these components into a simple instruction-set architecture. Iterative algorithms can then be expressed as programs executed by a transformer whose depth remains constant across loop iterations.

A single frozen transformer can, when given suitable input instructions, emulate a basic calculator, a linear algebra library, and an in-context learning algorithm that performs full backpropagation. These are constructive demonstrations of what specifically programmed looped transformers can compute. They illustrate how attention can support programmable operations and how input instructions can change the computation performed without changing the transformer's weights.
icml-2023-looped-transformers-as-program.tldr: Specifically programmed transformers can execute input-defined programs through looping, including calculations, linear algebra, and backpropagation.

paragraphs: A sequence predictor may need to adapt when the process generating its observations changes. This paper investigates whether memory-based neural models can learn that adaptation through ordinary sequential prediction training. Its motivation is that, under fairly general conditions, minimizing log loss leads to implicit meta-learning and can approximate a Bayes-optimal predictor.

The authors focus on piecewise stationary sources. Within each segment, the generating distribution stays fixed, but it changes at switching points that the predictor does not observe directly. Successful prediction therefore requires handling uncertainty about both the current segment's parameters and whether a change has occurred. The paper connects this setting to characteristics of language and partially observable interaction sequences.

The results show that Transformers, LSTMs, and RNNs can learn accurate approximations to known Bayes-optimal algorithms in the studied setting. Their behavior resembles Bayesian inference over hidden switching points and segment-specific parameters. This supports the interpretation that sequence training can produce adaptive inference behavior through memory, without establishing that every trained sequence model will develop the same capability.
icml-2023-memory-based-meta-learning-on-.tldr: Memory-based sequence models can learn to approximate Bayesian prediction when data distributions change at unobserved switching points.

paragraphs: This paper connects multicalibration, a collection of prediction consistency requirements, with boosting for regression under squared error. The authors first characterize multicalibration through a condition resembling swap regret. This creates a bridge between satisfying calibration requirements and repeatedly improving a predictor's squared-error performance.

Using that characterization, they develop a simple algorithm that can be understood both as regression boosting and as multicalibration for a function class H. It requires only a standard squared-error regression oracle for that class. Under a stated weak learning assumption on H, the algorithm converges to Bayes-optimal prediction without assuming that the ideal prediction function belongs to the chosen model class.

The weak learning condition is central to the guarantee. The authors prove it is both necessary and sufficient for multicalibration with respect to H to imply Bayes optimality. They also show that an appropriate relative weak learning condition transfers multicalibration from H to another class C. Alongside these theoretical connections, the paper investigates the algorithm experimentally, bringing calibration and agnostic regression boosting into a shared framework.
icml-2023-multicalibration-as-boosting-f.tldr: A shared algorithm links multicalibration and regression boosting, with Bayes-optimality guarantees governed by a necessary and sufficient weak learning condition.

paragraphs: Deep Q-learning methods have succeeded in decision-making applications, but their theoretical behavior is less well understood. This paper studies fitted Q-iteration with a two-layer ReLU neural network representing the Q-function. The Q-function describes the value of taking an action in a state, so learning it is central to choosing useful actions.

The proposed approach estimates that function at each iteration through a convex optimization problem. The authors analyze how many samples the resulting algorithm needs to reach a desired accuracy. They obtain a sample complexity proportional to the inverse square of the error tolerance, up to logarithmic factors, and establish that this rate is order-optimal.

The stated result applies to countable state spaces and does not require a linear or low-rank structure for the underlying Markov decision process. That scope matters because the guarantee does not depend on imposing either of those structural simplifications. The contribution is a sample-efficiency guarantee for the particular fitted Q-iteration approach studied, connecting neural function representation with a convex estimation procedure.
icml-2023-on-the-global-convergence-of-f.tldr: A convex-estimation version of fitted Q-iteration with two-layer ReLU networks achieves an order-optimal sample-complexity guarantee.

paragraphs: User-level differential privacy protects a user's contribution as a whole. This paper introduces a mechanism for stochastic convex optimization with that form of privacy guarantee. Its convergence rates are similar to prior results, but it broadens the kinds of losses the mechanism can handle and improves the stated requirement on the number of users.

The mechanism does not assume that the loss is smooth. Its bounds also make the minimum required number of users independent of the problem dimension, with only logarithmic dependence on the desired excess error. This is specifically a statement about that minimum-user requirement, rather than a claim that every aspect of the optimization problem becomes dimension-independent.

The technical idea concerns strongly convex losses: their optimizers have low local deletion sensitivity, meaning limited local change under deletion. The authors combine this property with a new output perturbation method for functions possessing that sensitivity property. This links control over how an optimizer changes with a way to privatize its output. The perturbation method may also be useful independently of the optimization mechanism.
icml-2023-on-user-level-private-convex-o.tldr: A user-private convex optimization mechanism removes smoothness assumptions and makes its minimum-user bound independent of dimension.

paragraphs: Stackelberg problems involve a leader whose choices account for how a follower responds. They arise in settings such as security games and indirect mechanism design. This paper presents a general framework for expressing the search for Stackelberg equilibria as a multi-agent reinforcement learning problem, making different algorithmic choices easier to organize and compare.

The authors show how previous approaches fit within the framework as particular instances. They also identify additional possibilities, including using multitask learning and meta-reinforcement learning to help followers converge. This is useful because the follower's learning behavior is part of the equilibrium-search process, so its implementation affects the overall procedure.

The paper develops one such approach using contextual policies and evaluates it on both established and newly introduced benchmark domains. It reports greatly improved sample efficiency relative to previous approaches. The authors also explore designs outside their framework. Together, the framework and experiments offer a way to structure equilibrium-search algorithms and evidence that a contextual-policy design can reduce the experience needed in the evaluated settings.
icml-2023-oracles-followers-stackelberg-.tldr: A general multi-agent RL framework enables a contextual-policy approach to Stackelberg equilibrium search with improved empirical sample efficiency.

paragraphs: Models can lose accuracy when deployed in environments unlike their training domains. This paper studies a subtle case: some features that change between domains still remain useful for prediction. In wildlife images, for example, backgrounds differ across camera locations but can reveal habitat, which helps identify the animals present.

The authors propose targeted augmentations that randomize misleading domain-dependent features while preserving useful ones. A theoretical analysis in a linear setting motivates this selective treatment. Within the studied analysis, they prove improved out-of-domain performance and better generalization with fewer domains. The key is to distinguish which changing features carry reliable information.

The paper contrasts this approach with generic augmentations that fail to randomize domain-dependent features and domain-invariant augmentations that randomize all of them. Both perform poorly out of domain in the comparison described. Experiments on three real-world datasets report improvements over the previous state of the art of 3.2–15.2%. These findings support designing augmentations around the predictive role of features, rather than treating all variation across environments alike.
icml-2023-out-of-domain-robustness-via-t.tldr: Selectively randomizing spurious features while preserving useful domain-dependent information improves generalization to unseen domains.

paragraphs: Assessing a self-supervised representation can be difficult when no labels are available. Joint-embedding methods do not reconstruct their inputs, so they offer no reconstructed images to inspect, and their loss values may reveal little about representation quality. This makes selecting a useful model on a new dataset particularly challenging.

RankMe uses the effective rank of learned representations as an unsupervised indicator of their quality. It provides a computationally friendly criterion without additional training or hyperparameters of its own. The authors show that it can help assess representation performance even when the eventual downstream dataset differs from the one used to learn the representation.

Across hundreds of training episodes, RankMe supports hyperparameter selection with almost no loss in final performance compared with selection procedures that use labels. This is an empirical result about the usefulness of the criterion, rather than an exact guarantee that rank determines task accuracy. Its practical contribution is a way to guide model selection in settings where labeled evaluation data is unavailable.
icml-2023-rankme-assessing-the-downstrea.tldr: RankMe uses representation effective rank to guide self-supervised model selection without labels or additional tuning.

paragraphs: Videos and other passive observations contain information about behavior, but often provide neither action labels nor rewards. This paper shows that such data can still support learning features that accelerate later reinforcement learning. It focuses on extracting useful structure from observations before an agent learns a downstream task.

The approach models intentions through changes in the likelihood of future outcomes when an agent acts toward a task. The authors propose a temporal-difference learning objective for learning about these intentions entirely from passive data. Optimizing it jointly produces representations of states, policies, and possible outcomes, linking what is observed with different ways behavior could influence the future.

The paper provides theoretical and empirical support that the learned features are suitable for value prediction on downstream tasks. Experiments demonstrate learning from several kinds of passive data, including videos involving different embodiments and YouTube videos. The result concerns learning useful representations without action or reward annotations; the reported benefit is that those representations make subsequent reinforcement learning more effective.
icml-2023-reinforcement-learning-from-pa.tldr: Learning latent intentions from passive observations produces representations that support value prediction and accelerate downstream reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Domain adaptation must handle changes in both how common classes are and how examples within each class appear. RLSbench evaluates this combined problem, called relaxed label shift. It contains more than 500 distribution-shift pairs across vision, tabular data, and language, with varying class proportions, providing a common basis for comparisons.

Evaluating 13 popular adaptation methods reveals more widespread failures under changing label proportions than previously recognized. The authors then propose a two-step procedure compatible with most domain adaptation heuristics. It first pseudo-balances the data at each training epoch, then adjusts the final classifier using an estimate of the target domain's label distribution.

Under large changes in label proportions, the procedure often improves existing heuristics by 2–10 percentage points of accuracy. When proportions do not shift, its reported effect is less than 0.5%. The benchmark and method together emphasize that adapting to changes within classes is only part of the problem: evaluations also need to test what happens when the relative frequency of classes changes.
icml-2023-rlsbench-domain-adaptation-und.tldr: RLSbench exposes adaptation failures under changing class proportions and introduces a two-step correction that often improves accuracy.

paragraphs: A reward model predicts preferences, but optimizing its score too aggressively can worsen the outcome it was intended to measure. This paper studies that mismatch quantitatively. To avoid the expense of repeatedly collecting human judgments, it uses a synthetic setup where a fixed gold-standard reward model supplies labels for training a proxy.

The authors optimize the proxy using either reinforcement learning or best-of-n sampling and track the resulting gold-model score. They find that the relationship follows different functional forms for the two optimization methods. In both cases, the fitted coefficients vary smoothly with the number of parameters in the reward model.

The study also examines reward-model dataset size, reward-model and policy size, and the strength of the KL penalty used during reinforcement learning. These empirical relationships help characterize how optimization pressure and model scale interact in this setup. Because the reference judge is itself a fixed model, the measured target is its score. The paper explores what these findings may imply for theoretical questions in AI alignment.
icml-2023-scaling-laws-for-reward-model-.tldr: A synthetic reward-model study finds method-dependent scaling relationships describing how proxy optimization affects a gold-standard model's score.

paragraphs: A useful representation may need to ignore some transformations while retaining information about others. Invariant representations stay unchanged under transformations, whereas equivariant representations change in a corresponding way. This paper seeks to combine these properties and bring equivariant self-supervised learning into larger, more varied evaluation settings.

The authors introduce 3DIEBench, containing more than 2.5 million rendered images across 55 classes, with control over transformations applied to the objects. They also develop a hypernetwork-based predictor designed to learn equivariant representations without collapsing into invariance. Their SIE method splits each representation into invariant and equivariant parts and combines that split with the predictor.

The paper reports significant qualitative and quantitative gains over existing methods on tasks related to equivariance. It also analyzes how the predictor shapes the learned latent space. The split gives the model separate places to represent information that should remain stable and information that should track transformations. The results support richer self-supervised representations for these tasks, while the dataset provides controlled transformations for studying that behavior.
icml-2023-self-supervised-learning-of-sp.tldr: SIE separates invariant and equivariant features and uses a hypernetwork predictor to improve performance on transformation-sensitive tasks.

paragraphs: This paper studies translation with a decoder-only transformer trained through self-supervision on unpaired language data. At inference time, the model receives a small set of high-quality translation examples. The authors demonstrate the potential of this approach for both high-resource and low-resource language pairs, separating general language training from the examples used to guide translation.

With five translation demonstrations, the models can match specialized supervised state-of-the-art systems and general commercial translation systems in the reported evaluations. On the WMT'21 English-Chinese news translation task, the approach outperforms the best-performing system using only five parallel examples at inference. The resulting models are also two orders of magnitude smaller than state-of-the-art language models.

The quality of the demonstrations strongly influences translation quality, making example selection central to the approach. Demonstrations can also guide particular output attributes: the authors show control over regional varieties and formality with five examples. The findings therefore concern both translation performance and a practical mechanism for steering how a translation is expressed through the examples supplied.
icml-2023-the-unreasonable-effectiveness.tldr: Five high-quality translation examples can guide self-supervised models to strong translation performance and control regional variety or formality.

paragraphs: Formal verification needs specifications describing which predictions or behaviors should be considered correct. Existing neural-network specifications often use small neighborhoods around reference inputs. This paper's empirical study finds those verified regions can be too narrow to cover test inputs, limiting their usefulness in some applications.

The authors propose specifications based on neural activation patterns, using internal network representations to describe regions for verification. They introduce a statistical method for discovering these patterns. For the resulting patterns, they formally verify properties including the impossibility of certain kinds of misclassification and the absence of ambiguity between different patterns. These guarantees apply to the specified patterns and properties.

On MNIST, the approach verifies a significant input-space region while retaining 84% data recall. On CIFAR10, the authors report extending the verifiable bound by a factor of ten. The results suggest that activation-based specifications can cover more useful regions than the input-neighborhood approach examined. The paper presents them as a potentially more reliable and extensible basis for neural verification.
icml-2023-towards-reliable-neural-specif.tldr: Specifications built from neural activation patterns enable formal verification over broader regions in the reported MNIST and CIFAR10 evaluations.

paragraphs: Directed graphs encode relationships whose orientation matters, as in source code and logic circuits. Although transformers have been applied across many data types, the paper identifies directed graphs as comparatively underexplored. It asks how to give a transformer information about both graph structure and the directions of its connections.

The authors propose two positional encodings. One uses eigenvectors of the Magnetic Laplacian, a direction-aware extension of the combinatorial Laplacian. The other uses directional random walks. Both provide ways to represent structural information that distinguishes directed relationships, allowing directionality to become part of the information available to the transformer.

Experiments show that the additional directional information helps on tasks including sorting-network correctness testing and source-code understanding. Combined with a graph construction centered on data flow, the model improves over the prior state of the art on Open Graph Benchmark Code2 by 14.7% relatively. That headline result belongs to the combined model and graph construction, while the broader experiments support the usefulness of direction-aware encodings.
icml-2023-transformers-meet-directed-gra.tldr: Direction-aware positional encodings help transformers model directed graphs, with a combined approach reporting a 14.7% relative Code2 improvement.
